title: A burial mound on the Dardanelles coast matches ancient descriptions of Ajax's tomb
dek: Archaeologists have identified a constructed mound near the ancient settlement of Rhoiteion. Its location and erosion damage align with classical accounts of the hero's monument.
body: Ten kilometres from the citadel of Troy, on the shore of the Dardanelles, a mound called Işıldaktepe Altı has been losing ground to the sea for decades. When archaeologists Fecri Polat and Rüstem Aslan first recorded it in 2011, they suspected a Copper Age settlement lay beneath the surface. The waves had other ideas, stripping away the flank to reveal something built, not grown.

The exposed face shows rows of stones set in mud, capped by a layer of greenish clay. The team argues this stonework was engineered to buttress an artificial heap of earth and stop it sliding toward the water. Pottery, spindle whorls, bone tools and fragments of large storage jars came from the slope, but the mound itself is not a habitation site. It is a deliberate burial monument.

The position is the clue that caught the researchers' attention. The mound stands beside the ruins of Rhoiteion, exactly where Greek and Roman writers placed the Tomb of Ajax. Strabo, writing in the early first century AD, notes the tomb in this stretch of the Troad. Later sources say the sea damaged the monument and that the emperor Hadrian ordered its repair.

Ajax the Great, the towering shield-bearer of the Iliad, was said to have died by his own hand after the war. His tomb became a landmark for sailors on the Hellespont. The fact that Işıldaktepe Altı sits on the active shoreline, its stones still spilling into the surf, echoes those ancient reports of a monument gnawed by waves.

No inscription names Ajax. No human remains have been reported from the mound's interior. The central core, where a primary burial would lie, has not yet been opened. Polat, writing in the Troy Museum Journal, stresses that the identification rests on geography and ancient testimony, not on recovered evidence from the grave itself.

Even a confirmed link would not make the Homeric warrior historical. Hero shrines and empty tombs for mythic figures dotted the Greek world. They served as focal points for cult and memory, not necessarily as repositories for bones. The mound could be a later construction honouring a story already centuries old.

What the site does offer is a rare chance to watch a legendary landscape feature emerge from the sediment. The Troad is thick with places tied to the Trojan War by tradition. Excavating the untouched centre could date the monument's construction and reveal whether antiquity genuinely knew this spot as the Tomb of Ajax.
doesnt_show: The mound has not yielded an inscription, datable material from the primary construction phase, or human remains that could identify a specific burial.
settle: Full excavation of the central chamber and scientific dating of the mound's construction layers would test the link to ancient accounts.
